s01.slug: FRIDAY · 4:50 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
body: The holy day is going out of the front window a few minutes at a time. By a quarter to five the sky over the roofs across Glenwood is the same gray as the snow along the curb — two inches fell before breakfast, and it has been plowed against and walked on ever since — and the tree is lit anyway, every bulb. One more week.

At ten it was Mary, Mother of God at St. Brigid’s, half the South Side in the pews in last night’s clothes. The first reading was Numbers — *The LORD bless you and keep you!* — and Fr. Dom, who has never in his life been able to leave a blessing alone, put his hand up over the pews at the end and gave it to them again. Gina slept on Jack’s shoulder through the naming in Luke with her mouth a little open, and woke for the Creed and got every word.

Now it’s Pasadena on the television. Frank is in his chair in the Buckeyes sweatshirt he takes out one day a year and which is, by now, mostly lint. Ma has the dish towel over her shoulder and the arm of his chair for a seat. Gina has the arm of the couch and the Flip. Rosie is on her stomach on the rug with the blue crab under one elbow and a bowl under the other, and in the window chair, under Theo’s cashmere, Nonna sits up straight with her beads in one hand and a spoon in the other and her eyes on the pot.

The pot is on the coffee table on a trivet, brown and plain and steaming up the lamp: lentils. The rule is older than the house. First meal of the year, one spoon each, *per i soldi*, a lentil for every coin you want. Ma goes around the room with the ladle. Jack’s goes in. Gina’s goes in, with a face. Ma tastes her own for salt, because a rule is a rule but it’s also her pot, and Nonna, who won’t touch her own until everyone else has taken theirs, watches each spoon from the bowl to the mouth.

Rosie doesn’t eat hers. She counts them out onto the rim of her bowl, a lentil at a time, and sorts them by value. “That’s a quarter. That’s a dime. That one,” holding it up to the lamp, “is Canadian, so it’s only worth some.”
From his chair, eyes on the screen, Frank says, “Don’t let the hall see that. They’ll want dues.”
“That’s going in the documentary,” Gina says.

Ma comes to Frank’s chair last. He holds up his bowl without taking his eyes off Pasadena. “Two.” Ma looks at the bowl. She gives him two. In the window chair, Nonna’s eyes follow the second spoon down.

It’s a good first half, from where they sit. Pryor runs like he means it. Oregon comes out in a uniform that Frank looks at for some time before asking if they lost a bet, and everybody in the stands is in shirtsleeves in January, which he also takes personally. He coaches the set in single words — *Wrap. Eyes. Low.* — and Gina keeps the Flip on him through all of it. “For the extras,” she says, when he points out the lens. By the second quarter Nonna is asleep with the spoon still upright in her fist, in case there’s another round.

At the half the bands come out onto the grass, and Jack gets up. “Where are you going?” Gina says. “Garage.” “It’s *halftime*.” “That’s why.” He takes the Carhartt down off its hook in the hall and gets an arm into it. From there he can see the whole room: Rosie building her coins into a tower for the second half, and Frank at the halftime numbers, going down the column with his lips moving, checking the math.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:15 AM · THE FRONT ROOM → 4:40 PM · THE SIDE YARD AND THE GARAGE
body: The front window is going from black to gray at a quarter past seven when the tape in the kitchen clunks over to its other side. It’s Nonna’s cassette, the carols a cousin in Warren taped off the radio before Danny was born, with a hiss on it older than any of the children. It goes back in the drawer under the toaster tonight, till next December. This morning it’s on the counter by the bread box, turned up to where the front room can have it, and Nonna, in her chair by the window with her beads in her lap, hums along a half beat behind.

Rosie’s stocking is the last one left on the mantel’s row of hooks, and in the night it has been filled: torrone in its white box, a clementine with the leaf still on, a fistful of chocolate coins in gold foil. She has the haul laid out on the rug and is briefing the blue crab. “The Befana was too busy sweeping to go with the kings,” Rosie says. “She said she’d catch up. Then she couldn’t find them. So now she goes to everybody’s house, in case the baby’s there.” In her chair, Nonna’s beads go on under the tape.

Jack comes down the stairs at twenty past with something swinging from his fist. It was hanging off the knob of the back bedroom door when he opened it, by its own cuff: one of Danny’s old tube socks, white, two blue stripes at the top, the heel worn nearly through, and heavy at the toe. The stairs are the one country Nonna hasn’t entered since the fall, so the Befana has had help. He tips the sock over into his palm. Black, glittering, a dozen lumps the size of walnuts, so convincingly coal that his first thought is the furnace.
“Nonna,” Gina says from the stairs behind him, hair in a knot, one sock on. “That’s *coal*.”
Nonna doesn’t look up from the beads. “*Dolce.*”
Rosie’s head comes up out of the stocking. “Jack was *bad*?”
Nonna lifts her chin and thinks it over.
“*Un pochino.*”
He breaks a corner off the biggest lump and lifts it toward his mouth, in front of her, since that appears to be what is required.
“Eat an egg first,” Ma says from the stove.
“It’s tradition, Ma.”
“So’s breakfast.” He eats it anyway. It’s sugar: black sugar, burnt at the edges, with a little anise at the back of it.
Frank, who has been in the kitchen doorway for a minute with his coffee, just seeing, says, “She gave me coal in ’81. It wasn’t sugar.”
Nonna, not looking up: “*Te lo meritavi.*”
“You brought me home at one,” Ma says, with her back to them.
Frank looks at his coffee. “Twice.”
Rosie, who has walked the three kings across the house since the twenty-sixth, a shelf at a time, from the far end of the bookcase, sets them down the last inch at the manger.

At twenty to five the day is done with Youngstown, and Frank and Jack are in the side yard taking down the Madonna’s lights. She has stood in her bathtub since before Danny was born, the paint worn pale at the nose, and there is snow lying in her cupped hands. Frank empties them first, with one glove, before he touches a bulb. Then the blue string comes off her in a long rope, and Jack coils it on his hand and elbow, as he was taught at eight. “Over,” Frank says. “Under.” The lesson has not been revised.
In the front-room window Nonna knocks once on the glass with a knuckle and, when they look, mouths it at them: *Finito.* Christmas is done.

In the garage the colored lights come down off the pegboard a loop at a time, and when the dead blue bulb comes level with the vise Frank stops and unscrews it. He holds it up under the overhead and looks at it, and drops it in the coffee can of drywall screws. From the sound, it has company. Behind them the pegboard is bare again except for the painted outlines of the tools, hammer and level and the long wrench, each in its black, waiting.

The Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall, as it has for as long as Jack has been tall enough to be told not to open it. Frank opens it. The little light comes on. Where the Stroh’s were, there is Canada Dry, standing in rows, green and gold. Frank takes out two. He sets one on the bench by Jack’s elbow and sits down on his bucket by the heater with the other. The duct-taped chair is under three boxes of lights, and the only other seat is the paint bucket at the end of the bench. On the bench the radio is on low, a man in Niles selling gutters.
“Hall called,” Frank says, and cracks his can. “Nothing yet.”

response: Frank reads the side of his can, which has the ingredients on it. “Your mother likes the bubbles.” He drinks. The radio goes on under them, low, to nothing in particular.

choices.text: *Take the can. Sit on the paint bucket. Say nothing.*
response: He takes the can off the bench and thumbs the tab and sits down on the paint bucket, with the heater ticking at his shins. Two ginger ales. The gutters give way to a woman reading the weather. After a time Frank looks at the bare pegboard and says, to nobody, “Cruze. Sounds like a boat.”
“Mr. Broussard’s got the Saints,” Frank says. “I got this.” He lifts the can at the bare pegboard and drinks to it, and Jack takes his off the bench and does the same.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 9:50 AM · GLENWOOD AVENUE → PITTSBURGH INTERNATIONAL
body: At ten to ten the duffel is by the front door and the zipper won’t close over the sandwiches. There are three, in foil, labeled in Ma’s capitals — PITTSBURGH TO DENVER. DENVER TO SANTA BARBARA. IN CASE. — because the airlines, she has told the front hall, do not feed anybody.

Nonna doesn’t get up. Jack goes to her chair, and it takes her a long time to find the twenty. The left pocket of the housedress first, then the right, then the left again: a tissue, a holy card, a butterscotch in cellophane, a bead come off something, and last the bill, folded to the size of a stamp. “*Per il viaggio*,” she says, and closes his fingers on it with her hand over his. Then her thumb goes to his forehead and makes the cross there, hard enough to keep, and she tells him close, in Calabrese, and he gets every word of it.
“*Prego per tutt’e due.*”
A breath later: “*Anche per Cassidy.*”
He kisses her cheek. She smells of Jergens and radiator. Her hand is still on his sleeve when Ma calls him from the side door.

Ma has the dish towel on her shoulder and the can in both hands. It’s the Café du Monde can from the cupboard, empty, washed, the lid pressed back on. “For the girl who called,” she says. “Tell her it was good coffee. Those words.” It goes into the duffel on top of the sandwiches, and Ma watches it go in.

Gina and Rosie are waiting on the side step, and the door’s spring bangs shut behind him. Rosie has a drawing in both hands, in her church shoes, for the plane: a plane, with Jack in a window, and in the next seat the blue crab, belted in, reading. Under the crab, in her best printing, CALLINECTES SAPIDUS. “So you’re not by yourself,” she says.
“Who gets the window?” Jack says.
“You. He’s on the aisle, in case.”
Gina has the Flip up and the red light on. “I’m keeping the tape. ‘Say things out loud.’ You’re on it forever.”
“Is that thing ever off?” Jack says.

“Not till the credits.” At the bottom of the step she puts her free arm around his neck, hard, and says into his ear, so low it’s mostly breath: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Then she’s back behind the lens as if she’d said nothing at all.

Frank takes the turnpike at the speed limit, in the right lane, through flurries that come down dry across the wipers, with KDKA low on the dash giving the Steelers their offseason. Frank, a Browns man, endures it.

At Departures the Silverado stops where the sign says nothing stops. A man in an orange vest opens a conversation with the windshield, and Frank rolls the window down two inches and says, “Thirty seconds,” and rolls it up. He gets the duffel from the back seat himself and puts it in Jack’s hand. Then the hug, one arm, hard, the other hand on the roof of the truck.
“Call your mother when you land,” he says. “She don’t sleep.”
Jack nods. He has turned for the doors when Frank adds it, in the same tone. “And tell the TV one the Browns won four straight. She’ll want to know.”

The doors open for him without being asked. When he looks back through the glass, the Silverado is still at the curb with its hazards going, the man in the vest at the window again, and Frank, well past his thirty seconds, explaining something to him with one hand.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.”

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon. Counted her New Year’s lentils out like coins. Put the three kings at the manger on the sixth. Drew me a plane with the crab in the next seat.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.*

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first.
